items.followUp: Differentiate between a donor atom and an acceptor atom in a coordinate covalent bond.

rubric.why: Identifies the role of the donor atom.
rubric.description: A donor atom provides or donates a lone pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the donor provides the electron pair.

rubric.why: Identifies the role of the acceptor atom.
rubric.description: An acceptor atom accepts or receives the electron pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the acceptor receives the electron pair.

modelAnswer: A donor atom provides a lone pair of electrons for bond formation.
An acceptor atom receives that lone pair of electrons.

items.followUp: Define a double covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: States the defining feature of a single covalent bond.
rubric.description: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one pair of electrons is shared.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a molecule with a single covalent bond.
rubric.description: A correct example is H₂, Cl₂, or HCl.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving one correct example.

modelAnswer: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.
For example, the bond in an H₂ molecule is a single covalent bond.

items.followUp: What is a coordinate covalent bond? Give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies the type of bond present in a coordinate covalent compound.
rubric.description: A coordinate covalent compound contains a coordinate covalent bond with a shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the coordinate covalent bond and shared pair.

rubric.why: States the distinctive source of the shared electron pair.
rubric.description: Both electrons in the shared pair are donated by one atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one atom supplies both electrons.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent compound contains a bond in which a shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom.
Both electrons in the shared pair come from the donor atom.

items.followUp: Why does evaporation occur at temperatures below the boiling point?

rubric.why: Explains which molecules leave the liquid during evaporation.
rubric.description: Higher-energy molecules at the liquid surface escape into the air.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that higher-energy surface molecules escape.

rubric.why: Connects the escaping molecules to the cooling of the liquid left behind.
rubric.description: The remaining liquid has lower average kinetic energy, so its temperature decreases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the loss of higher-energy molecules to a temperature decrease.

modelAnswer: During evaporation, the higher-energy molecules at the surface escape from the liquid.
The remaining liquid has lower average kinetic energy, so its temperature decreases and it cools.
